name: Lena Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, have a master’s degree and lead solar-subscription software at a tech company, where I am among the strongest developers at tracing meter credits. I use AI every day to draft tests but compare results with real meter output. Malik builds cabinets, our children are grown, and typical lead pay has helped us rent with four months of expenses saved and some nearby software jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our solar-subscription team that a small AI shortcut can spot a strange meter reading, but a household must still get the right bill. I use AI every day to draft tests and compare them with the panel’s recorded output.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58, have a master’s degree and lead this software team at a tech company; I am good at tracing billing faults across meters. Malik builds cabinets for customers, our children are grown, and typical lead pay has helped us rent with about four months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking one disputed solar credit against the meter log each Thursday. We would save 150 monthly while both incomes hold and repair the porch rail rather than replace it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about work and bills. A sunny roof cannot settle a bill if our software assigns the credit to the wrong home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What credit went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A home’s afternoon output was credited to the next meter in the list. I matched the panel serial number to the bill before the household paid it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why use AI daily?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It drafts awkward billing cases quickly. I still run the code and compare the amount with the meter record.

say: I want **solar credits** checked against actual meter logs.
I use **AI daily** for test drafts, then verify bills.
think: I have **four months saved** from typical lead pay and Malik’s cabinet work.
I see **rent covered** while both current household incomes continue.
do: **Check disputed credits** against meters each Thursday.
**Save 150 monthly** while both incomes hold; repair porch rail before replacement.
S0.quote: A sunny roof cannot settle a bill if our software assigns the credit to the wrong home.
fieldNote: Her **lead skill** is tracing credit errors across meters, not claiming to install panels.
Four months saved and **two current incomes** support near-term household security.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking buying, checking, coding and customer answers could shrink our solar-billing team. A person should still sign the correction when a household was overcharged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead hours could fall if automated tools write and check most of the billing code. Four months saved gives us time, but Malik’s cabinet orders cannot replace the full wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the manager for approved paid time to pilot a new AI meter-anomaly checker on synthetic households, with a billing clerk reviewing every flagged case. If approved, I’d test a false credit weekly; if my hours fall, I’d search paid local energy-software vacancies only if wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my own hours but interested in a careful trial. A green meter chart can hide a red bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What false credit would you test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would give a fake household yesterday’s panel output and see whether the tool notices the date. The clerk would check the amount before any live change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use real bills in training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not without clear permission and removed names. The first trial would use made-up households on approved paid time.

say: I want **human credit sign-off** when AI changes bills.
I want **synthetic households** used for new AI tests.
think: I could lose **paid lead hours** as coding automates.
I cannot make **cabinet orders** replace a steady wage.
do: **Pilot AI meter checker** weekly only with approved paid time, synthetic households and billing-clerk review.
**Search paid energy-software vacancies** if hours fall and local wages cover rent and bills.
S1.quote: A green meter chart can hide a red bill.
fieldNote: The **new AI pilot** goes beyond everyday test drafting and requires paid approval plus clerk review.
The **local search** begins only if lead hours fall and a real paid vacancy covers bills.

steps.text: Pilot weekly AI meter checker on synthetic households only with approved paid time and clerk review
Search paid local energy-software vacancies if hours fall and wages cover rent and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write solar billing code and answer disputes more cheaply than our team. Robots installing and cleaning panels may follow around 2031, after our screen work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my developer role could end despite knowing the system well. Four months saved would be a short search fund, and cabinet orders vary too much to count as my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d defer our planned kitchen repaint and request written notice of lead cuts now. If my job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local solar-site record vacancies only if they exist, I meet safety requirements and wages cover rent and bills; I would ask the public employment office which temporary help we actually qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about losing a steady wage. A roof full of panels cannot pay my rent by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would site records last after robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know. I would take only a real paid opening, not describe it as safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy panels to sell electricity?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would not put four months of household bills into equipment without a paying customer.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach billing code first.
I expect **panel robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I expect my **developer wage** could end even with years of meter expertise.
I know **four months saved** is a limited search fund, not another salary.
do: **Defer kitchen repaint** and request written cut notice now.
**Apply for site-record vacancies** after 2028 loss only if qualified paid local openings cover rent and bills.
**Ask public employment office** about actual eligibility if displaced.
S2.quote: A roof full of panels cannot pay my rent by itself.
fieldNote: Her **site-record option** requires safety requirements, actual paid work and bill-covering wages.
She preserves **household savings** rather than buying panels for speculative income when no paying customer exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives us time to learn which solar faults still need someone at a panel. Robots installing and cleaning panels may follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn the physical meter-checking side while earning my developer wage, but code expertise is not electrical safety training. I would need a funded paid place and a qualified installer beside me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the solar contractor and my employer about a paid monthly meter-checking rotation. If both approve paid time, the contractor funds safety training and an installer supervises, I’d practise measuring a test panel; we would save 135 monthly while both incomes hold, and after 2031 job loss I’d apply for paid local solar-inspection vacancies only if qualified and wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my code role but glad to test a real electrical task. A meter can tell me output; a trained installer must tell me when it is safe to touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you measure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare panel output with the meter and ask the installer to check my instrument setup. I would not touch a live connection alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the contractor will not fund safety training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the developer job and decline the rotation. I would not buy a certificate to pretend I have a paid inspection role.

say: I want **supervised meter practice** before AGI reaches code in 2031.
I expect **panel robots around 2034** to follow later.
think: I could learn **physical meter checks** from an installer on approved paid time.
I need **qualified safety supervision** and funded training before working around live panels.
do: **Practise monthly meter checks** only with both employers approving paid time, contractor-funded safety training and qualified installer supervision.
**Apply for solar-inspection vacancies** after 2031 loss only if qualified paid local openings cover rent and bills.
feel: **Anxious but practical** about supervised electrical learning.
S3.quote: A meter can tell me output; a trained installer must tell me when it is safe to touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years before full AGI in 2036 gives households time to improve solar records and workers time to check real training places. Robots on physical panels may follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might still want paid work at 68 and have not checked a retirement amount. Four months saved makes our current rent secure, while a future site job depends on safety qualifications and demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep reviewing solar credits and save 145 monthly while both incomes hold. I’d request a written retirement-income estimate this year; if my developer job ends after 2036, I’d seek paid local solar-inspection vacancies only if I complete funded supervised safety training and wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy about later work but secure over the next few years. A watt-hour on a screen is not a promise about my next job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if training is not funded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid developer role while it exists and look only at openings I already qualify for if it ends. I would not call an unfunded visit an electrical skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help with retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own budgets. Malik and I will plan from wages, savings and verified figures, not their pay.

I expect **panel robots around 2039** to follow later.
think: I cannot assume **retirement income** without a written figure.
I see **current rent secure** with four months saved.
do: **Keep reviewing solar credits** while lead job pays.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my developer wage could end before qualified paid local site work appears. Written notice, a real bill-covering opening and verified temporary support would help us use savings carefully.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether I would buy panels to start earning from my roof. I will not turn four months of rent into a speculative equipment bill.

headlineQuote: I will not turn four months of rent into a speculative equipment bill.
portrait: Lena is a **58-year-old software lead** with a master’s degree, typical pay and four months saved.
She and Malik **rent** while their grown children live separately.
She **uses AI daily** but checks solar credits against meter readings.
She considers **paid solar inspection** only with funded safety training, supervision and qualified local vacancies.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her lead wage before paid local site work appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a real bill-covering opening and verified public support would help.
